note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — OPEN, NOT COMPACT
tiles.details: Actual field photo (gallery panel 1) shows a tightly converging living bunch near soil level, but exposed root fibers and the buried basal rhizome are not pictured. Gallery panels 2–3 show OPEN widely branching flowering heads (not a compact fluffy head); panel 7 reinforces how widely separated flowering branches carry spikelets. Published GrassBase under synonym Tridens buckleyanus describes a broad 10–28 cm mature panicle and 4–13 cm lateral branches, not measurements independently made from these photos. Gallery panels 9–10 add a physically collected Bandera compact leafy base and exposed dry sheaths; short rootlike strands are not a cleaned measured root network.
tiles.short: Broadly ovate 10–28 cm panicle with widely spaced, spreading or ascending 4–13 cm branches.
tiles.status: REAL SPECIES HABIT PANELS — SAME-PLANT PANICLE SCALE STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE LIGULE AND COLLAR
tiles.details: The exact source-licensed Eric Knight photograph (gallery panel 4) shows a green leaf joining the culm near its node. On the inspected pixels this is a visible leaf attachment/culm NODE region, NOT an opened sheath with a clearly resolved free ciliate ligule; the earlier generic blade–sheath terminology overstated the image. A true species-specific 0.4–1 mm ciliate membrane requires gently peeling open the inner sheath of a verified flowering plant and focusing beside a 1-mm ruler. Gallery panel 11 is a Bandera blade/sheath transition, panel 12 is a separate Hays County local collar region. Neither actually isolates or measures the short true inner ciliate ligule.
tiles.short: A 0.4–1 mm ciliate membranous ligule is a PUBLISHED trait, not photographically measured here.
tiles.status: LEAF ATTACHMENT/TRUE CULM NODE VISIBLE — INNER LIGULE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS; SEPARATE BOTH GLUMES
tiles.details: Gallery panels 5–8 show real source-determined Buckley spikelets: attached mature units, a detached spikelet, attached flowering units and an enlarged whole mature unit. They do NOT establish measured individual glumes or floret count, and should not include the panel 4 leaf/node picture. Published GrassBase measurements under historical Tridens buckleyanus describe 7–10 mm spikelets, 3–5 fertile florets, lower persistent glume commonly 5–6 mm and upper 4–5 mm; verify in several ripe spikelets with a 1-mm scale only when distinguishing the overlapping slim Tridentopsis.
tiles.short: Spikelets 7–10 mm with usually 3–5 fertile florets; lower glume 5–6 mm, upper 4–5 mm.
tiles.status: REAL SPIKELET PHOTOS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTION WITH 1-MM SCALE

tiles.heading: 04 · THREE-VEINED LEMMA; NO LONG AWN
tiles.details: GrassBase describes a blunt or notched lemma apex, awnless or only minutely mucronate. Isolate one mature floret to show the lemma's dorsal face, its basal hairs, and the palea. The available overview/spikelet images cannot verify submillimeter hairs or the exact lemma tip. No microscopic arrows are justified until pixels resolve those structures.
tiles.short: Fertile lemma 4–6 mm, three-veined, hairy low on midvein and margins; palea 3–5 mm.

tiles.heading: 05 · LOCAL LOOK-ALIKES — SLIM TRIDENTOPSIS
tiles.details: Panels 13–15 show Tridentopsis mutica, NOT Buckley. Five florets and 8–10 mm spikelets overlap, so these measurements alone do not confirm species. Compare complete same-scale panicles, branch angles, glume proportions, and verified lemma hair distribution. Tridens texanus and airy Eragrostis can also mislead; color is not a reliable separator.
tiles.short: Buckley: open spreading head, often 3–5 florets; slim: 0.3–0.8 cm-wide contracted head, often 5–11.
tiles.status: REAL OTHER-SPECIES COMPARISON — OVERLAP REQUIRES MATURE DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / TWO HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one connected rooted live perennial with exposed knotty crown/short rhizome and full open 10–28 cm panicle; opened true inner 0.4–1 mm ciliate membranous ligule beside 1-mm scale; three ripe 7–10 mm spikelets with measured glumes, floret counts and three-veined hairy lemma only when slim tridens overlap persists. NEEDS_SITE_QA: 12 existing exact-species JPEGs (seven CC BY and five CC BY-NC) plus three explicitly OTHER-SPECIES slim tridens comparison panels, all 15 panel indices, actual visible arrow endpoints and rights-filtered mobile display. Aboveground sheaths and a Hays County collar-region photograph do NOT establish a measured free ligule or exposed connected rhizome. Preserve provisional taxonomy/native-range holds.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: 12 archived Buckley JPEGs, 15 panels total; true measured ligule and connected rooted crown still missing.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: BUCKLEY TRIDENTOPSIS (Buckley tridens): look for an OPEN, broadly ovate panicle whose straight primary branches spread or ascend well away from the axis, with small separated spikelets. The original card's 'compact/fluffy' shortcut is inconsistent with the existing photo and Kew GrassBase. Verify 3–5 fertile florets, usually 7–10 mm spikelets and dorsal lemma hairs on an intact mature specimen; county-native certification stays provisional.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: 1 · Ground-level bunch: use gallery panel 1 (Sam Kieschnick), whose actual pixels show a green/dry leaf tuft anchored in soil. Soil conceals actual root crown and short rhizome; do not point at a presumed underground organ. New panels 9–10 show close hand-held basal sheaths and basal fibers from the same Bandera source observation, but no rooted crown/rhizome with a scale.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The exact source-licensed Eric Knight photograph (gallery panel 4) shows a green leaf joining the culm near its node. On the inspected pixels this is a visible leaf attachment/culm NODE region, NOT an opened sheath with a clearly resolved free ciliate ligule; the earlier generic blade–sheath terminology overstated the image. A true species-specific 0.4–1 mm ciliate membrane requires gently peeling open the inner sheath of a verified flowering plant and focusing beside a 1-mm ruler. Gallery panel 11 is a Bandera blade/sheath transition, panel 12 is a separate Hays County local collar region. Neither actually isolates or measures the short true inner ciliate ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Gallery panels 5–8 show real source-determined Buckley spikelets: attached mature units, a detached spikelet, attached flowering units and an enlarged whole mature unit. They do NOT establish measured individual glumes or floret count, and should not include the panel 4 leaf/node picture. Published GrassBase measurements under historical Tridens buckleyanus describe 7–10 mm spikelets, 3–5 fertile florets, lower persistent glume commonly 5–6 mm and upper 4–5 mm; verify in several ripe spikelets with a 1-mm scale only when distinguishing the overlapping slim Tridentopsis.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Compared with T. mutica, the best gross clue is a spreading, open panicle rather than a slender column of closely ascending branches. Buckleyana tends 3–5 florets/spikelet versus 5–11 in mutica, but 5 overlaps; lengths overlap at 8–10 mm. Verify by dissection, not head shape alone. Historical Tridens buckleyanus is a synonym, not another species card.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 1 · IN SITU TUFT — photographed grass base, roots not excavated
panels.caption: Sam Kieschnick's original CC BY 4.0 field photograph, inspected from its true image bytes at a scaled 675×900 preview, shows a distinct tight grass tuft with many narrow leaves at ground level. The arrow identifies only the visible convergence of grass blades in the soil-level bunch. It is NOT a photograph of bare fibrous roots, knotty rhizome, or a measured inner ligule. Flowering culms occur in the scene but cannot be confidently connected to one photographed root crown.

intro: BUCKLEY TRIDENTOPSIS (Buckley tridens): look for an OPEN, broadly ovate panicle whose straight primary branches spread or ascend well away from the axis, with small separated spikelets. The original card's 'compact/fluffy' shortcut is inconsistent with the existing photo and Kew GrassBase. Verify 3–5 fertile florets, usually 7–10 mm spikelets and dorsal lemma hairs on an intact mature specimen; county-native certification stays provisional.
memory_rule: BUCKLEYANA = OPEN SPREADING; MUTICA = TIGHT UPRIGHT. Confirm 3–5 versus 5–11 florets and lemma nerve hairs; 5 overlaps.
safety_note: Fifteen comparison gallery panels = twelve archived same-species photos including conditional CC BY-NC + three DIFFERENT-SPECIES slim Tridentopsis photos. Original panel 4 is culm/node, newer panels 11–12 show blade/sheath transitions but not a measured free 0.4–1 mm ligule. New hand-held basal photos show tight live/dry tillers and short basal strands, NOT exposed same-vouchered roots/rhizome plus cm scale. FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
field_rule: Do not finalize at species if whole-panicle context is absent or floret count sits in overlapping range; dissect true ripe spikelet with scale.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

Historical Tridens buckleyanus is a synonym, not another species card.
